speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Transport with the reopening of Changi Airport’s Terminal 4 and the recommencement of departure operations in the southern wing of Terminal 2 (a) what is the total number of additional manpower required to support the reopening; (b) whether the terminals are sufficiently manned to meet Singapore’s year-end air passenger traffic targets; and (c) if not, how does the Ministry ensure that there is sufficient manpower to support the ramp-up in capacity so that travellers’ experience that Changi Airport is renowned for is not affected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked 	the Minister for Transport with the gradual reopening of terminals at Changi Airport (a) what percentage of its capacity is the airport operating at presently, taking into account the airport’s currently available manpower, retail services and other infrastructure; (b) what are the assumptions underlying the projection that the number of flights handled by Changi Airport will rise to 80% of pre-pandemic levels by end-2022; and (c) what concrete steps are being taken to scale up on the airport’s capacity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Iswaran, will you be taking Question Nos 14 and 15 together?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Yes, I am taking Question Nos 14 and 15 together, please, Speaker.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Air travel has recovered steadily since Singapore reopened its borders to all fully vaccinated travellers without testing or quarantine in April 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The number of flights at Changi Airport has also recovered to nearly two-thirds of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The number of flights that airlines have filed to operate at Changi Airport by the year end is more than 80% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We expect this to increase further as airlines respond to demand from travellers, following the recent border-easing announcements by key travel markets such as Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To accommodate this anticipated growth in the number of passengers and flights, we reopened Terminal 4 on 13 September.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will also be commencing departure operations in the southern wing of Terminal 2 on 11 October, in addition to arrivals which had commenced on 29 May.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This also represents about 80% of Changi’s pre-COVID-19 capacity itself.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, we have used the intervening time to enhance Changi's capacity as well.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our aviation stakeholders have been concurrently working hard to build up their workforce and train their new hires to support this ramp-up in capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This has been an ongoing process since early this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The air transport sector workforce has recovered to about 80% of pre-COVID-19 levels in the first half of the year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Cumulatively, this will bring us to about 90% of our pre-COVID-19 workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The recruitment efforts of the companies in the sector are currently on track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And thanks to the efforts of the whole aviation community, including our regulator, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS), airport operator, airlines, ground handling companies, unions and workers, Changi has managed the recovery relatively well so far.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: By continuing to work together as one Changi community, we are confident that Changi Airport will be ready to welcome more passengers back to Singapore and offer them the distinctive traveller experience that Changi is known for.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that Changi Airport is our strategic asset and has still many labour-intensive components, such as baggage handling, catering and training, what lessons can be learnt and incorporated in the future Terminal 5 (T5) design and possible retrofitting of the current infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And how can we provide more support for the airport workers, such as those represented by Singapore Airport Terminal Services Workers Union (SATSWU) to upskill and improve productivity so that we can continue to improve on the renowned service of Changi Airport?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of upgrading and upskilling the workers, this is an ongoing effort.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As with all other sectors in Singapore, it is a priority because, ultimately, by upskilling the workers, we enhance their productivity, enhance the competitiveness of the companies and the larger aviation sector and, of course, enable them to have good jobs with good wages.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is a virtuous cycle, something that we are continually working on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member's first question was on areas such as baggage handling and what lessons we have learnt that can be incorporated into the T5 design.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The last two years, as Members would know, we had paused in the development of T5 because the trajectory of air travel recovery was uncertain in light of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the key lessons we have learnt include how we can modularise airport operations in order to enhance their resilience – in this case, our civilian airport – to such pandemic-type challenges.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because, as I think all of us would well appreciate, airports are designed for convergence of streams of passengers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And yet, when you are in a pandemic-type situation, the objective is really to separate the streams as much as we can according to their risk categorisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That inverts the logic of airport operations and is something that has to be factored into the design early, not just in terms of processes, but in terms of actual physical design.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, modularity and how it can help combine with processes to enhance the resilience of our airport in the face of possible pandemics in the future is one aspect.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And finally, on specific areas like baggage handling which the Member raised, this is actually one of the key challenges and this is not unique to Changi.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because all over the world, baggage handling is one of the most manpower-intensive aspects of airport operations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: How we are able to automate this is a key part of the work that is going on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As I think Members can well appreciate, this is not something you can decide on a standalone basis because it is not only one airport doing this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whatever we do has to be ultimately coordinated with airlines, aircraft design and what happens in other airports.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a general effort that is being undertaken to see how greater automation can be brought into the handling of baggage at airports.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is an ongoing effort and CAAS is investing in a lot of innovation work in that regard.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First one is: would Minister envisage the possibility of overshooting the capacity over the next few months into the end of this year and possibly into the first half of next year, particularly if regional airports or other hubs, are seeing any delays in their opening?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And that also is in relation to one of my Parliamentary Questions (PQs): what would be the assumptions underlying the projection that the number of flights will rise to 80% and above?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second supplementary question would be: the Minister mentioned that the recruitment is on track, but is it possible for us to speed up the recruitment of talent, especially since technology and changes over the past two to three years have evolved, and whether some of these technological changes mean that we need new talent locally or globally coming to Singapore?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On overshooting capacity, I think what the Member meant by that is whether we expect that we will go beyond what we think is the expected volume.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To some extent, there is predictability and the reason why there is predictability is because airlines file their flight plans with the airport slots authority, that is, with Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this case, for the next cycle which is really from October through to March next year, it is called the Northern Winter schedule.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: From that point of view, we already have a reasonable idea of the kind of flows to expect.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Of course, there may be variations to that for a variety of reasons, whether it is disruptions and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But by and large, given what has been presented to our airport, we think that the estimations that we have are within the ballpark.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Whether it will exactly turn out the way we expect, I think there are many unknowns, as all of us will appreciate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Minister for Health talked about some of the risks as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We need to just bear in mind that we plan with the capacity in mind, but we also need to be vigilant and be prepared to pivot to a more conservative and careful stance if the need arises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, of course, the assumptions that the Member asked about – that underlie this planning, apart from what the airlines submit and so on – is, of course, in general, how the source markets are opening up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In particular, in our part of the world, the Asia Pacific, most have opened up, as I mentioned earlier – Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong and so on have all opened up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One of the most significant markets is China and China's opening strategy is something that we have to observe, because every country has to navigate this path based on its circumstances.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is a major uncertainty as well that we will have to watch out for.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The second point on recruitment and whether we speed up the recruitment, I can assure the Member that all the aviation companies are throwing the kitchen sink at this because this is a very challenging time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the end of last year, we had about 25,000.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of new talent, that really is going to be an important area of focus going forward because of two aspects.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Digitalisation and sustainability are going to be key drivers for the aviation industry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For this, we will need specific skill sets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have to retrain those who are already in the industry and that is happening as we speak.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At the same time, we also may need specific types of talent to come on board to augment what we already have.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And so, this is something that both the airlines but also the airport and ground handlers are focused on.
